lesson.title: Tempo, Dynamics and Articulation
lesson.summary: Italian words and a few signs tell how fast, how loud and how connected the music should be.

section.title: Tempo
section.p: Tempo is the speed of the beat. Composers usually give it with an Italian word at the start of the piece, sometimes with a metronome mark: a quarter note = 120 means 120 quarter-note beats per minute.
The common tempo terms, roughly from slowest to fastest:

list.li: Allegretto: moderately fast, a little slower than allegro.

section.p: Sources do not agree on the order of the slow terms largo, lento and adagio, and the speeds changed between periods. The terms describe a character as much as a speed.
Other words change the tempo along the way:

list.li: A tempo: back to the previous tempo.
Rubato: with flexible tempo, pushing ahead and holding back for expression.

check.explanation: Ritardando means gradually slower. Accelerando is the opposite, and a tempo returns to the earlier tempo after such a change.

check.prompt: Which of these tempo terms is the fastest?
check.explanation: Presto means very fast. Allegro is fast, and allegretto a little slower than allegro.

section.title: Dynamics
section.p: Dynamics are the loudness of the music. They are written as letters standing for Italian words, usually below the staff (above it in vocal music), from very soft to very loud:
Even softer and louder levels add more letters, such as ppp and fff. Dynamics are relative: forte on a flute is not as loud as forte on a trumpet.

Gradual changes are written as words or as hairpins. A crescendo (cresc.), a hairpin opening to the right, means gradually louder; a diminuendo (dim.) or decrescendo, a hairpin closing to the right, means gradually softer.
Sudden changes have their own signs. Sforzando (sfz or sf) is a sudden strong accent on one note or chord; fp means loud and then immediately soft; subito means suddenly, as in subito piano.

check.explanation: Mezzo means moderately: mezzo-piano is moderately soft and mezzo-forte moderately loud, so mp is the softer of the two.

check.prompt: A hairpin below the staff opens wider from left to right. What does it mean?
check.explanation: A hairpin that opens to the right is a crescendo: the music grows louder as the lines spread apart. A hairpin that closes is a diminuendo. Hairpins never show tempo.

section.title: Articulation
section.p: Articulation tells how notes begin, end and connect. Most articulations are signs placed above or below the notehead:

list.li: Staccato, a dot: short and detached.
Staccatissimo, a small wedge: very short.
Tenuto, a short horizontal line: held for its full value, often with slight weight.
Accent, the sign >: played with emphasis.
Fermata, an arc over a dot: a pause; the note or rest is held longer than written, as long as the performer judges.

section.p: Legato means smoothly connected, with no gap between the notes. It is usually shown with a slur, a curved line over or under notes of different pitches.

check.prompt: A dot is placed above a notehead. What does it mean?
check.option: Play the note short and detached
Make the note half as long again
Play the note with an accent
check.explanation: A dot above or below the notehead is a staccato. A dot after the notehead is a rhythmic dot, which makes the note half as long again.

section.title: Other common directions
section.p: A few small words combine with the terms above:

list.li: Molto: very, much. Poco: a little. Poco a poco: little by little.
Più: more. Meno: less. Sempre: always. Non troppo: not too much.
Dolce: sweetly. Cantabile: in a singing style. Espressivo (espr.): expressively. Con moto: with motion.

section.p: Some directions tell the player where to go next:

list.li: Dal segno (D.S.): from the sign, an S with a slash and two dots.
Fine: the end. Da capo al fine means: go back to the beginning and play up to Fine.
Coda: a closing section. The jump to it is marked with the coda sign, a circle crossed by two lines.

step.p: A piece starts with Allegro non troppo: fast, but not too fast.
The first phrase is marked p and dolce: softly and sweetly.
Later comes cresc. poco a poco: grow louder little by little, until the next dynamic mark. A rit. near the end slows down gradually, and an a tempo afterwards returns to the opening speed.

check.prompt: What does poco a poco cresc. mean?
check.explanation: Poco a poco means little by little, and cresc. gradually louder: the music should grow louder slowly over several notes or bars.

check.prompt: What does D.C. al fine tell the player to do?
check.option: Go back to the sign and play to the end
Go back to the beginning and play up to Fine
Play the last section again more slowly
check.explanation: Da capo means from the beginning, and al fine up to the word Fine, where the piece ends. Going back to the sign would be dal segno.
